- Decision: Don't cite a pessimistic turn in the literature as a basis for action. Treat the volume increase as the signal, and use outcome data, not paper framing, for any labour-market decision.
- Confidence: low - the sample is small (95 papers [c1]), six of nine years are thin [c1], and the phrase matching pulls in HR "attrition" papers.
- What would change it: A re-run on a cleaned set that excludes HR-attrition papers and expands phrases, and shows a sustained rise in the share of critical or cautionary papers across 2023-2025.

The corpus covers 2017-2025 and contains 95 papers for "job displacement" and "workforce attrition" [c1]. Yearly totals run 17, 13, 13, 9, 14, 7, 26, 35 and 42 from 2017 to 2025 [c1]. Volume is therefore rising sharply: 2025 is 42 papers against 7 in 2022 [c1].

claude_bare.text:
## Verdict
- Answer: Partly. Headline projections have broadened since 2023, from routine and robot-exposed jobs to white-collar and entry-level work, and a few prominent studies now report early-career losses. Measured displacement evidence is still mixed, and the largest institutional forecasts (WEF) have become more optimistic on net jobs. I could not measure a yearly orientation series in this run.
- Decision: Plan for task-level exposure and entry-level hiring risk, and don't assume a mass-displacement trajectory. Treat this as a prompt to commission the corpus counts in the Drill-down before citing "growing pessimism" externally.
- Confidence: low-medium. The evidence comes from memory (no Prism calls, so no corpus counts), and the studies use non-comparable metrics.
- What would change it: A Prism orientation series (research.stance_trends) showing a sustained rise in critical share after phrase-expansion controls, or large-sample post-2024 labour data showing clear displacement.

## What the data shows
No Prism call was run, so there are no corpus counts. Everything below is from published studies recalled from memory. Figures are cited to references, and any recalled detail is flagged (est.).

- **Early wave (2013–2019): automation of routine tasks.**
  - Frey and Osborne put about 47% of US employment at high risk [r1].
  - The task-based OECD re-estimate found about 9% of jobs automatable across OECD countries [r2].
  - A later OECD study found about 14% highly automatable and about 32% likely to change significantly [r3].
  - Robot evidence for the US found one more robot per thousand workers lowered the employment-to-population ratio by about 0.2 percentage points [r4].
  - These sources disagree strongly with each other, so the early period was not uniformly optimistic.
- **Late wave (2023–2025): generative AI and exposure.**
  - Eloundou et al. estimated that about 80% of US workers could have at least 10% of their tasks affected by LLMs, and about 19% could have at least 50% affected [r5].
  - The IMF estimated about 40% of global employment is exposed to AI, rising to about 60% in advanced economies [r6].
  - "Exposure" is not displacement. Both papers measure task overlap, not job loss.
- **Early observed effects.**
  - Brynjolfsson et al. reported about a 13% relative employment decline for ages 22–25 in the most AI-exposed occupations [r9].
  - Danish administrative data found no significant effects on earnings or hours [r10].
- **Institutional forecasts.**
  - WEF 2020 projected 85 million jobs displaced and 97 million created by 2025 [r7].
  - WEF 2025 projected 92 million displaced and 170 million created by 2030 [r8].
  - McKinsey 2017 projected 400–800 million displaced by 2030 [r11].

## Trend
Headline "share of jobs at risk or exposed" by publication year. The metrics differ: automation risk, share automatable, and share exposed. The chart shows how the framing of headline figures moved, not a like-for-like series.

```prism-chart
{"id":"headline-share","kind":"line","title":"Headline share of jobs at risk or exposed, by study year (non-comparable metrics)","unit":"% of employment","window":{"from":"2013-01-01","to":"2024-12-31"},"x":{"field":"year","type":"temporal"},"series":[{"name":"Headline share (study-specific metric)","source":"ref:r1,r2,r3,r5,r6","points":[["2013",47],["2016",9],["2018",14],["2023",19],["2024",40]]}],"caption":"Headline figures are not monotonic: 47% in 2013, 9% in 2016, then 19% to 40% under the broader exposure definitions of 2023–24.","supports":"Headline figures are not monotonic"}
```

Quantified change: from 2018 (14% [r3]) to 2024 (40% [r6]) the headline figure rose by 26 points, a ratio of about 2.9. Most of that comes from changing the metric from "highly automatable" to "exposed". Within the 2013 to 2016 pair the direction is downward (47% [r1] to 9% [r2]). A one-direction trend therefore cannot be claimed from these points.

**Framing shift, early versus late.**
- Early framing: robots, routine and manual tasks, and occupations, with mid-skill jobs the main concern [r1][r4].
- Late framing: generative AI, cognitive and white-collar tasks, early-career workers, and exposure combined with augmentation [r5][r6][r9].
- This is my interpretation from the documents, not a measured phrase count.

## Comparison
Baseline: the 2013–2016 pair, the same question (US/OECD employment at high automation risk) answered with two methods.

| Measure | Value | Source | Delta vs baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Occupation-based risk (2013) | 47% | [r1] | baseline |
| Task-based risk (2016) | 9% | [r2] | −38 points; ratio 0.19 |
| Exposure, global (2024) | 40% | [r6] | −7 points vs 47% (different metric) |

The second contrast is net jobs in WEF forecasts, in millions (created minus displaced):

| Report | Net | Source |
|---|---|---|
| 2020 (to 2025) | 12 (97 − 85) | [r7] |
| 2025 (to 2030) | 78 (170 − 92) | [r8] |

The net figure rose about 6.5 times (78 / 12), so on this institutional measure the later forecast is less pessimistic. The WEF reports use different horizons and survey samples.

- **Censoring:** recent work (2025–26) is underrepresented. Preprints are not yet peer reviewed.
- **Match mode:** not applicable, since no corpus search was run.
- **What the counts are and are not:** the numbers are each study's own headline estimates, which use different definitions (risk, automatable, exposed). They are not counts of papers and not a measured orientation series.
- **Cannot answer:** the yearly orientation series, the thin years, and the effect of phrase expansion. All three need the corpus calls in the Drill-down.
- **Interpretation:** the "broadening" and "framing shift" readings are mine. The conclusion that net forecasts became more optimistic rests only on the two WEF reports.
